newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN report says U.S. undermining Cuban dissenters.
newsitem.headline: UN report says U.S. undermining Cuban dissenters.

text.p: A United Nations investigator said on Thursday U.S. measures aimed at weakening communist rule in Cuba could undermine a growing dissident movement on the island and lead many dissenters to emigrate.

In a report for the world body's Human Rights Commission, Swedish lawyer Carl-Johan Groth also suggested renewed pressure from the United States had led President Fidel Castro to take a tougher line on any suggestion of democratic reform.

And he said the fact that economic crisis in the early 1990s had not led to a collapse of Castro's administration indicated it had greater support among all parts of the Cuban population than outside observers had believed.

Under 1996 legislation tightening its embargo on Cuba, "the United States assumes the right to be the outside party that determines the rules for converting the current totalitarian system into a different, more pluralist one," Groth declared.

"This inspires doubt rather than confidence about the future and may cause some dissidents to feel that their own criteria are irrelevant and that Cuba's future will be decided in any case without consulting them.

"The direct result of this situation could be a decline in the trend towards overt political activity and the risk it implies," said Groth, who was refused permission by Havana to make a study visit to the island for his report.

And in the present political environment, he added, "the Cuban government has taken a frankly negative, not to say hostile, attitude towards the idea of introducing a pluralistic political system in Cuba."

The lawyer, who in previous reports for the Commission over the past few years has often suggested U.S. policy towards Cuba was counter-productive, said Castro's administration continued to violate human rights by suppressing dissent.
During 1996, he said, dissident groups had been subjected to intensive harassment.

"Threats, intimidating visits to the homes of political activists and the imposition of penalties for alleged economic crimes which are in fact political activities are the methods used by the authorities in their effort to break up any form of opposition," declared Groth.

But he said information he had gathered from Cuban exiles in the United States and other countries and from indirect contacts with dissenters on the island suggested the number of trials and the length of sentences had been reduced.

This trend, he said in an implicit barb at U.S. refusal to talk to Havana, seemed partly due to "the critical dialogue in which a number of countries and regional groups, in Europe and Latin America, have engaged Cuba."

The European Union, Canada and Latin American countries have objected strongly to the latest U.S. moves against the island, arguing that critical discussion and contact with Havana on rights is more productive than open economic pressure.

The EU, backed by many other trading powers, has brought a case against Washington in the World Trade Organisation, arguing that the 1996 Helms-Burton act aimed at reducing foreign investment in Cuba violates the body's rules.
Despite reduced judicial action, Groth said, human rights groups and individual activists in Cuba still deserved "all the protection the international community can provide.
"To be a dissident in Cuba is as difficult and risky today as it has been at any time in recent years," he added.
